  • Low sunlight: at low irradiance the pump speed falls (and the flow with it), and below a threshold the pump stops.
  • No battery: the water is stored in a tank instead of a battery, which reduces cost.
  • Result: the pump delivers the water in proportion to the sunlight and the panel works near its maximum power.

docs.title: Q214. Do you need a starter in a drive consisting of a permanent magnet motor directly connected to the battery? (Dubey 9.4) (10 marks · Module 5 · End Sem)
docs.text:
• Starting current: at standstill \(E=0\), so \(I=\frac{V}{R_a}\) is very large for a small armature resistance.
  • Direct connection: the battery would supply this high current, which may damage the brushes and the commutator.
  • Battery limit: a battery has internal resistance, which limits the current to a degree, but not enough for a large motor.
  • Small motors: for very small motors with a relatively high resistance, no starter is needed.
  • Large motors: a starter (series resistance, or a chopper that increases the voltage gradually) is needed.
  • Torque: the starting torque is proportional to the current, so it is high, but jerky.
  • Chopper starting: a chopper provides soft starting with a smooth rise in speed, and no resistor loss.
  • Efficiency: a resistance starter wastes energy and is less efficient, so a chopper is preferred.
  • Protection: a current limit and a battery fuse protect the system.
  • Answer: yes for all but the smallest motors, and the best starter is a chopper (electronic starter).

docs.title: Q215. What are the advantages and disadvantages of using a battery in a solar pump drive? (Dubey 9.5) (10 marks · Module 5 · End Sem)
docs.text:
• Advantage – steady supply: the battery smooths out the cloud effects, so the pump gets a steady voltage.
  • Advantage – extended hours: the pump can run in the evening or at night and in weak sunlight.
  • Advantage – starting: the battery supplies the high starting current of the motor.
  • Advantage – simple motor: a motor with a simpler controller can be used, as the voltage is fixed.
  • Disadvantage – cost: the battery adds a large initial cost and a replacement cost.
  • Disadvantage – maintenance: the battery needs maintenance and has a short life (3 to 5 years).
  • Disadvantage – efficiency: it adds charge and discharge losses, which lower the overall efficiency.
  • Disadvantage – MPP: the panel is not always at its maximum power point, since the battery sets the voltage.
  • Disadvantage – size: more weight, volume and a charge controller are needed.
  • Alternative: using a water tank to store the water (instead of storing electricity) avoids most of these disadvantages.

docs.title: Q216. What are the advantages and disadvantages of an electric vehicle compared with an internal combustion vehicle? (Dubey 9.6) (10 marks · Module 5 · End Sem)
docs.text:
• Advantage – emissions: zero tail-pipe emission, so it is good for city air quality.
  • Advantage – noise: quiet, with little vibration.
  • Advantage – efficiency: the drive efficiency is high (about 80 to 90%), against about 25% for an engine.
  • Advantage – regeneration: braking energy can be recovered, which extends the range.
  • Advantage – torque and control: instant torque from standstill, and simple control with no gearbox or clutch.
  • Advantage – maintenance: fewer moving parts and no oil changes.
  • Disadvantage – range: the energy density of batteries is low, so the range is limited.
  • Disadvantage – charging: it takes a long time to recharge, and charging stations are limited.
  • Disadvantage – cost and weight: the battery is heavy and expensive, with a limited life.
  • Disadvantage – grid dependence: the pollution moves to the power station if the grid is fossil fuelled.

docs.title: Q217. Draw the circuit diagram and explain the operation of a battery-powered dc series motor drive for an electric vehicle without facility for regenerative braking. (Dubey 9.7) (10 marks · Module 5 · End Sem)
docs.text:
• Supply: a battery of fixed voltage \(V\) feeds the drive through a contactor (main switch).
  • Power circuit: a chopper (thyristor or transistor \(S\)) is in series with the series motor, whose armature and field are in series.
  • Freewheeling diode: a diode \(D\) across the motor provides a path for the motor current when \(S\) is off.
  • Motoring operation: when \(S\) is on, the battery voltage is applied and the current rises; when \(S\) is off, the current freewheels through \(D\) and falls.
  • Average voltage: \(V_a=dV\) with \(d\) the duty ratio, so the motor speed and torque are controlled by \(d\).
  • Starting: the chopper starts at a small duty ratio, which limits the current, and the duty ratio is raised as the speed rises (no starting resistor).
  • Series motor features: a high starting torque (\(T\propto I^2\)), and the speed falls as the load rises, which suits traction.
  • Reversal: a changeover contactor reverses the field connections to run in reverse (the armature current direction is fixed).
  • No regeneration: since the current can flow only from the battery to the motor, braking energy cannot be returned, and braking is mechanical (or dynamic with a resistor).
  • Control: the accelerator pedal sets the duty ratio, with current limit and battery protection.

docs.title: Electric Drives — Mid Sem
Syllabus
docs.text:
1. DC motor characteristics — emf/torque equations, torque-speed curves, armature voltage control, flux weakening
  2. Chopper fed DC drive — duty ratio control, steady-state operation, current ripple, losses & efficiency
  3. Multi-quadrant DC drive — four-quadrant operation, 1/2/4-quadrant choppers, regenerative braking
  4. Closed-loop control of DC drive — inner current & outer speed loop, dynamic model, transfer functions
  5. Induction motor characteristics — equivalent circuit, torque-slip, fan/pump loads, flux weakening
  6. Scalar (V/f) control — 3-phase VSI, PWM/SVM, steady-state V/f analysis
  7. Slip ring induction motor control — rotor resistance control, slip power recovery

Main textbook: Fundamentals of Electrical Drives — G.K. Dubey

docs.title: Q1. Describe the 4-quadrant operation of an electrical drive. (5 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
An electric drive operates across four distinct quadrants on the torque-speed (\(\omega-T\)) plane, determined by the polarities of rotational speed and electromagnetic torque.

Illustration: 4-Quadrant Drive Operating Characteristics on the Torque-Speed Plane

docs.title: Detailed Technical Explanation
docs.text:
An electric motor can operate either as a motor (converting electrical power to mechanical power) or as a generator/brake (converting mechanical power back to electrical power or heat). The operational quadrant is dictated by the direction of angular speed \(\omega\) and developed electromagnetic torque \(T\):

  1. Quadrant I — Forward Motoring:

    • Conditions: Angular speed \(\omega > 0\) and developed torque \(T > 0\).
    • Power Flow: Mechanical power \(P = T \cdot \omega > 0\) (power is transferred from the source to the mechanical load).
    • Practical Example: An electric train or EV accelerating forward on a level track, or a crane hoist lifting a loaded container upwards.

  2. Quadrant II — Forward Braking (Regenerative / Generating):

    • Conditions: Angular speed \(\omega > 0\) and developed torque \(T < 0\).
    • Power Flow: Mechanical power \(P = T \cdot \omega < 0\) (energy is extracted from the moving kinetic load and returned to the electrical supply).
    • Practical Example: An electric vehicle braking while moving forward, or an electric locomotive decelerating down a steep slope.

  3. Quadrant III — Reverse Motoring:

    • Conditions: Angular speed \(\omega < 0\) and developed torque \(T < 0\).
    • Power Flow: \(P = (-T) \cdot (-\omega) > 0\) (power is delivered to drive the mechanical load in reverse).
    • Practical Example: A rolling mill reversing direction or an EV driving in reverse gear.

  4. Quadrant IV — Reverse Braking:

    • Conditions: Angular speed \(\omega < 0\) and developed torque \(T > 0\).
    • Power Flow: \(P = T \cdot \omega < 0\) (the motor produces positive torque opposing reverse motion to decelerate the load).
    • Practical Example: Controlled lowering of an empty hoist cage where gravitational torque acts in the reverse direction.

Source: G.K. Dubey, Fundamentals of Electrical Drives, Ch. 1

docs.title: Q2. Derive the torque-speed equation for a separately excited DC motor. (5 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
The steady-state torque-speed characteristic of a separately excited DC motor reveals an inherently linear speed-droop relationship governed by armature resistance and field excitation flux.

Illustration: Separately Excited DC Motor Equivalent Circuit Schematic

docs.title: Mathematical Derivation
docs.text:
Assumptions:

  • Steady-state operating conditions with pure DC supply.
  • Constant field excitation current (\(I_f = \text{constant} \implies \Phi = \text{constant}\)).
  • Negligible armature reaction demagnetization effect.

Step 1: Armature Circuit Voltage Balance Equation The applied terminal voltage \(V\) supplies the induced back EMF \(E_b\) and the ohmic voltage drop across armature winding resistance \(R_a\): $$ V = E_b + I_a R_a $$ where \(I_a\) is the armature current.

Step 2: Induced Back EMF Relation The back EMF generated in the rotating armature conductors cutting magnetic flux is: $$ E_b = K_b \Phi \omega = K \Phi \omega $$ where \(K = \frac{P Z}{2 \pi A}\) is the machine structural constant, \(\Phi\) is the magnetic flux per pole in Webers, and \(\omega\) is the rotor speed in rad/s.

Step 3: Electromagnetic Developed Torque Relation The electromagnetic torque developed by the interaction of flux and armature current is: $$ T = K_t \Phi I_a = K \Phi I_a $$ Solving for armature current \(I_a\): $$ I_a = \frac{T}{K \Phi} $$

Step 4: Substitution into Voltage Equation Substitute the expressions for \(E_b\) and \(I_a\) into Step 1: $$ V = K \Phi \omega + \left(\frac{T}{K \Phi}\right) R_a $$

Step 5: Final Governing Torque-Speed Equation Rearranging to solve for angular speed \(\omega\): $$ \omega = \frac{V}{K \Phi} - \frac{R_a}{(K \Phi)^2} T $$

docs.title: Analytical Interpretation:
docs.text:
• Ideal No-Load Speed (\(\omega_0\)): At zero developed torque (\(T = 0\)): $$ \omega_0 = \frac{V}{K \Phi} $$

  • Speed Droop Slope: The speed falls linearly with increasing load torque with a slope equal to: $$ m = -\frac{R_a}{(K \Phi)^2} $$ Because \(R_a\) is typically very small in modern industrial DC machines, the slope is slight, providing an almost constant (stiff) speed characteristic across rated load.

Source: G.K. Dubey, Fundamentals of Electrical Drives, Ch. 2

docs.title: Q3. Explain the principle of regenerative braking in a chopper-fed DC drive. (5 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
Regenerative braking in a chopper-fed DC drive operates on the step-up (boost) chopper principle, allowing mechanical kinetic energy from the rotating motor to be boosted and fed back into the main DC power source.

Illustration: Step-Up Chopper Topology for DC Motor Regenerative Braking

docs.title: Operating Principle & Circuit Action
docs.text:
During regenerative braking, the motor field remains excited while the armature acts as a DC generator with induced EMF \(E_b\). The circuit behaves as a boost converter consisting of the motor back EMF \(E_b\), series smoothing inductor \(L\), power semiconductor switch (chopper \(CH\)), and freewheeling feedback diode \(D\):

  1. Mode 1 — Chopper ON (\(0 \le t \le t_{on}\)):

    • Switch \(CH\) is closed. Current flows from the motor armature \(E_b\) through inductor \(L\) and switch \(CH\), completing the loop.

    • Energy is extracted from the rotating kinetic mass of the motor and stored in the magnetic field of inductor \(L\): $$ E_b = L \frac{di_a}{dt} + R_a i_a $$

    • Armature current rises linearly, developing an opposing electromagnetic braking torque (\(T = K\Phi I_a\)).

  2. Mode 2 — Chopper OFF (\(t_{on} \le t \le T\)):

    • Switch \(CH\) is opened. Because inductor current cannot drop discontinuously, the voltage across inductor \(L\) reverses polarity (L Lenz's law).
    • The combined induced voltage \((E_b + L \frac{di_a}{dt})\) exceeds the DC supply voltage \(V\).
    • Feedback diode \(D\) becomes forward-biased, forcing the stored energy and generated current to flow directly back into the DC supply \(V\).

Average Armature Terminal Voltage: $$ V_a = (1 - \delta) V $$ where \(\delta = \frac{t_{on}}{T}\) is the chopper duty ratio. By dynamically varying the duty ratio \(\delta\), the effective braking torque and braking speed can be precisely regulated down to very low speeds.

Source: G.K. Dubey, Fundamentals of Electrical Drives, Ch. 3

docs.title: Q4. Explain scalar (V/f) speed control of a 3-phase induction motor. (5 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
Scalar \(V/f\) control regulates the synchronous speed of a 3-phase induction motor by varying stator frequency while simultaneously adjusting terminal voltage to maintain constant magnetic flux in the core.

Illustration: Induction Motor Torque-Speed Curves under Variable Frequency (V/f) Control

docs.title: Theoretical Analysis & Working Principle
docs.text:
The synchronous speed \(\omega_s\) of a 3-phase induction motor with \(P\) poles supplied at frequency \(f\) is: $$ \omega_s = \frac{4\pi f}{P} \quad (\text{or } N_s = \frac{120 f}{P}) $$ Thus, motor speed can be smoothly controlled by altering the stator frequency \(f\).

Why Voltage Must Be Adjusted With Frequency (\(V/f = \text{constant}\)): From Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the induced stator EMF \(E_1\) is related to air-gap flux \(\Phi_m\) by: $$ E_1 = 4.44 \cdot k_w \cdot f \cdot N_{ph} \cdot \Phi_m \implies \Phi_m \approx \frac{V_1}{4.44 \, k_w \, N_{ph} \, f} \propto \frac{V_1}{f} $$

  1. If Frequency Decreases with Constant Voltage:
    • The flux \(\Phi_m \propto \frac{V}{f}\) would increase rapidly.
    • This drives the magnetic core into deep magnetic saturation, causing excessive magnetizing current, severe overheating, and high harmonic distortion.
  2. If Frequency Increases with Constant Voltage:
    • The flux \(\Phi_m\) decreases, causing a steep decline in maximum breakdown torque (\(T_{max} \propto \Phi_m^2\)).

docs.title: Operating Regions:
docs.text:
• Region 1 — Sub-Base Speed (\(f \le f_{base}\), Constant Torque Region):
    • Both voltage and frequency are scaled proportionally: \(\frac{V_1}{f} = \text{constant}\).
    • Air-gap flux \(\Phi_m\) is held constant at rated value.
    • Maximum breakdown torque \(T_{max}\) remains constant across this speed range.
    • Voltage Boost at Low Frequencies: At very low frequencies (\(< 15\text{ Hz}\)), stator resistance drop \(I_1 R_1\) becomes significant compared to \(E_1\). An additional voltage offset (voltage boost) is applied to maintain rated flux.
  • Region 2 — Above Base Speed (\(f > f_{base}\), Field Weakening Region):
    • Stator voltage reaches rated insulation limit (\(V_1 = V_{rated}\)) and cannot be increased further.
    • Only frequency \(f\) is increased. Consequently, flux weakens (\(\Phi_m \propto \frac{1}{f}\)), and maximum torque decreases proportionally to \(\frac{1}{f^2}\) (constant power mode).

Source: G.K. Dubey, Fundamentals of Electrical Drives, Ch. 5

docs.title: Embedded System — Mid Sem
Syllabus
docs.text: Practice these questions only.

docs.title: Q1. Identify the components of an embedded system. (2 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
Illustration: block view of an embedded system

  • Hardware: processor or microcontroller, memory (ROM / Flash and RAM), sensors and input devices, actuators and output devices, timers, ADC / DAC and I/O ports, plus clock, reset and power supply.
  • Software: firmware (and an RTOS if used) stored in memory, which makes the hardware perform its one dedicated task.

docs.title: Q2. What are the various classifications of embedded systems? (2 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• By generation and complexity: 1st generation (4/8-bit), 2nd (8-bit microcontrollers), 3rd (16/32-bit, DSP, ASIC) and 4th (SoC, multicore); also small-scale, medium-scale and sophisticated systems.
  • By behaviour and use: real-time (hard and soft) versus non-real-time, event-triggered versus time-triggered, and standalone, networked or mobile systems.

docs.title: Q3. Identify the different processors used in embedded systems. (2 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Processing units: general purpose microprocessor, microcontroller (8051, PIC, AVR, ARM) and digital signal processor (DSP).
  • Application specific and programmable: ASIC, ASIP, FPGA / PLD and System on Chip (SoC).

docs.title: Q4. Define interrupt latency. (2 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Interrupt latency is the time from the arrival of an interrupt request to the first instruction of its interrupt service routine (ISR).
  • It includes finishing the current instruction, saving the context, fetching the vector address, and any time interrupts are masked. A smaller value means a faster response.

docs.title: Q5. Differentiate between CISC and RISC processors. (2 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• CISC: large, complex instruction set with variable length instructions; many addressing modes; most instructions access memory and take several clock cycles; fewer registers (e.g. 8051, x86).
  • RISC: small, simple instruction set with fixed length instructions; few addressing modes; only LOAD / STORE access memory and most instructions take one cycle; many registers and easy pipelining (e.g. ARM, AVR, PIC).

docs.title: Q6. What are the important embedded processor chips? (2 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• 8-bit and 16-bit controllers: Intel 8051, PIC (Microchip), AVR (ATmega328), TI MSP430, Motorola 68HC11.
  • 32-bit, DSP and IoT chips: ARM Cortex-M (e.g. STM32), TI TMS320 DSP, ESP8266 / ESP32.

docs.title: Q7. Draw and compare the von-Neumann and Harvard architectures. (5 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
Illustration: von Neumann (one memory, one bus) and Harvard (separate memories and buses)

  • Memory: von Neumann uses one memory for program and data; Harvard uses separate program and data memories.
  • Buses: von Neumann has one shared address and data bus; Harvard has separate buses for each memory.
  • Speed: in von Neumann an instruction fetch and a data access cannot overlap (bus bottleneck); in Harvard they happen in parallel, so it is faster and suits pipelining.
  • Hardware: von Neumann is simpler and cheaper; Harvard needs more buses and pins, so it is more complex.
  • Use: von Neumann in general purpose computers (x86); Harvard in microcontrollers and DSPs (8051, PIC, AVR).

docs.title: Q8. Explain in detail about interrupt latency and its solutions. (5 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
Illustration: timeline from interrupt request to ISR and back

  • Meaning: interrupt latency is the delay between the interrupt request and the first instruction of the ISR.
  • Causes: finishing a long current instruction, interrupts masked in a critical section, a higher-priority interrupt running first, and memory wait states.
  • Fixed overheads: saving the context (PC, flags, registers) and fetching the ISR address from the vector table.
  • Solution 1: keep the ISR short (do urgent work only, defer the rest to the main program) and keep interrupt-disabled sections short.
  • Solution 2: use priorities and nested interrupts, a vectored interrupt controller, register banks for fast context switch, fast memory for the vector table and ISR, and DMA to avoid an interrupt per byte.

docs.title: Q9. Illustrate briefly the various memories used in embedded systems. (5 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• ROM family (non-volatile): masked ROM (factory programmed) and PROM (user programmed once).
  • EPROM and EEPROM: EPROM is erased by UV light; EEPROM is erased electrically byte by byte, used for small settings.
  • Flash: erased in blocks; the most common memory for firmware.
  • RAM (volatile): SRAM is fast with no refresh, used for registers and small data memory; DRAM is dense and cheap but needs refresh.
  • Others: NVRAM / FRAM (keeps data without power), cache (small and very fast), CPU registers and external storage such as SD cards.

docs.title: Q10. Illustrate the simple view of the organization of processor and memory in a system. (10 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
Illustration: CPU, memory, I/O and the three buses

  • Control unit: decodes each instruction and generates the timing and control signals.
  • ALU: performs arithmetic and logic operations on the data.
  • Registers: the accumulator and general registers hold working data.
  • PC and IR: the program counter holds the address of the next instruction; the instruction register holds the one being executed.
  • SP, MAR and MDR: the stack pointer points to the top of the stack in RAM; the memory address register holds the address to access; the memory data register holds the data read or written.
  • Program memory: ROM / Flash stores the firmware instructions.
  • Data memory: RAM stores variables, the stack and temporary results; I/O ports and timers are reached through the same buses.
  • Address bus: one way, CPU to memory and I/O; \(n\) lines can address \(2^n\) locations.
  • Data bus and control bus: the data bus carries instructions and data both ways; the control bus carries read, write, clock, reset and interrupt signals.
  • Working: the cycle is fetch (PC address, read the instruction into IR, PC increments), decode, execute (ALU, store the result), then repeat.

docs.title: Q11. Explain the functional difference between timers and counters. (10 marks · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
Illustration: the same count register driven by a clock (timer) or by external events (counter)

  • Common hardware: both are a register that counts up (or down) one step for every pulse it receives; only the pulse source differs.
  • Timer clock source: the register is clocked by the internal clock, which has a fixed, known frequency, often through a prescaler.
  • Timer function: because the pulse period is known, the count measures time: time = count × clock period.
  • Timer events: it overflows or matches a compare value after a fixed time and can raise an interrupt.
  • Timer uses: delay generation, periodic tasks, baud-rate generation, PWM and watchdog.
  • Counter clock source: the register is clocked by an external signal on a pin, on each rising or falling edge.
  • Counter function: the pulses can arrive at any rate, so the count measures the number of events, not time.
  • Counter uses: counting products on a conveyor, shaft revolutions or measuring the frequency of a pulse signal.
  • Mode selection: a control bit selects timer or counter mode (e.g. the C/T bit in the 8051 TMOD register).
  • Link between them: a counter fed with a signal of known frequency works as a timer, which is why one unit does both jobs.

docs.title: Essential Studies for Professionals VII — Mid Sem
docs.text:
Revision set, not a question bank

No question bank was available for this paper. These questions are my own picks from the syllabus (GATE Electrical, Power Systems and Power Electronics), ordered by how testable the topic is. Check anything unusual against your class notes.

docs.title: Syllabus
docs.text:
1. Power Systems: bus admittance matrix, Gauss-Seidel and Newton-Raphson load flow, voltage and frequency control, power factor correction, symmetrical components, symmetrical and unsymmetrical fault analysis, overcurrent / differential / distance protection, circuit breakers, stability concepts, equal area criterion.
  2. Power Electronics: characteristics of diode, thyristor, TRIAC, GTO, MOSFET, IGBT; buck, boost and buck-boost converters; single and three phase uncontrolled rectifiers; line commutated thyristor converters; bidirectional AC to DC converters; line current harmonics, power factor, distortion factor; single and three phase inverters; sinusoidal PWM.

Reference: GATE Electrical Engineering (G.K. Publications), Chapters 5 and 10.

docs.title: Q1. Explain symmetrical components and write the transformation equations. (5 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Idea: any unbalanced set of three phasors can be split into three balanced sets: positive, negative and zero sequence.
  • Positive sequence: three equal phasors 120° apart in the normal order a-b-c.
  • Negative sequence: three equal phasors 120° apart in the reverse order a-c-b.
  • Zero sequence: three equal phasors in phase with each other.
  • Equations: with \(a=1\angle120^\circ\), \(V_a=V_0+V_1+V_2\), \(V_b=V_0+a^2V_1+aV_2\), \(V_c=V_0+aV_1+a^2V_2\), and \(V_0=\tfrac13(V_a+V_b+V_c)\), \(V_1=\tfrac13(V_a+aV_b+a^2V_c)\), \(V_2=\tfrac13(V_a+a^2V_b+aV_c)\).

docs.title: Q2. Show how the sequence networks are connected for LG, LL and LLG faults. (5 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Sequence networks: each of positive, negative and zero sequence has its own network, with the source only in the positive one.
  • LG fault: the three networks are in series, so \(I_{a1}=I_{a2}=I_{a0}=\dfrac{E}{Z_1+Z_2+Z_0}\) and \(I_f=3I_{a0}\).
  • LL fault: only positive and negative networks are used, in parallel, with \(I_{a0}=0\) and \(I_{a1}=-I_{a2}=\dfrac{E}{Z_1+Z_2}\).
  • LLG fault: all three networks are in parallel, with \(I_{a1}=\dfrac{E}{Z_1+\dfrac{Z_2Z_0}{Z_2+Z_0}}\).
  • 3-phase fault: only the positive network is used, with \(I_f=E/Z_1\).

docs.title: Q3. A generator has \(E=1\) pu, \(Z_1=Z_2=j0.2\) pu and \(Z_0=j0.1\) pu. Find the fault current for a single line-to-ground fault. (5 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Series connection: for an LG fault the three sequence networks are in series.
  • Total impedance: \(Z_1+Z_2+Z_0=j0.2+j0.2+j0.1=j0.5\) pu.
  • Sequence current: \(I_{a1}=\dfrac{E}{j0.5}=-j2\) pu, and \(I_{a2}=I_{a0}=I_{a1}\).
  • Fault current: \(I_f=3I_{a1}=-j6\) pu.
  • Answer: the fault current is \(6\) pu, lagging the voltage by 90°.

docs.title: Q4. Form the bus admittance matrix for a 3-bus system with line impedances \(j0.1\) (1-2), \(j0.2\) (1-3) and \(j0.05\) (2-3) pu. (5 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Line admittances: \(y_{12}=\dfrac1{j0.1}=-j10\), \(y_{13}=-j5\), \(y_{23}=-j20\).
  • Diagonal terms: each is the sum of the admittances connected to that bus, so \(Y_{11}=-j15\), \(Y_{22}=-j30\), \(Y_{33}=-j25\).
  • Off-diagonal terms: each is the negative of the line admittance, so \(Y_{12}=j10\), \(Y_{13}=j5\), \(Y_{23}=j20\).
  • Matrix: \(Y_{bus}=j\begin{bmatrix}-15&10&5\\10&-30&20\\5&20&-25\end{bmatrix}\).
  • Check: the matrix is symmetric and every row sums to zero, because there are no shunt elements.

docs.title: Q5. Compare the Gauss-Seidel and Newton-Raphson load flow methods. (5 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Gauss-Seidel: solves \(V_i^{(k+1)}\) bus by bus from the latest values. It is simple and needs little memory.
  • Gauss-Seidel convergence: linear, so it needs many iterations, and the count grows with the number of buses.
  • Newton-Raphson: linearises the power equations and solves \(\begin{bmatrix}\Delta P\\\Delta Q\end{bmatrix}=J\begin{bmatrix}\Delta\delta\\\Delta|V|\end{bmatrix}\) with the Jacobian \(J\).
  • Newton-Raphson convergence: quadratic, so it usually converges in 3 to 5 iterations, independent of system size.
  • Choice: Newton-Raphson is preferred for large systems because each iteration costs more but far fewer are needed.

docs.title: Q6. State the swing equation and explain the equal area criterion. Derive the critical clearing angle. (10 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Swing equation: \(\dfrac{H}{\pi f}\dfrac{d^2\delta}{dt^2}=P_m-P_e\), where \(H\) is the inertia constant in MJ/MVA.
  • Power-angle: \(P_e=P_{max}\sin\delta\).
  • Meaning: if \(P_m>P_e\) the rotor accelerates, and if \(P_m<P_e\) it decelerates.
  • Stability idea: after a fault the rotor must be able to swing back before it loses synchronism.
  • Equal area criterion: the system is stable if the accelerating area \(A_1\) equals the decelerating area \(A_2\).
  • Accelerating area: \(A_1=\int_{\delta_0}^{\delta_c}(P_m-P_e)\,d\delta\), during the fault.
  • Decelerating area: \(A_2=\int_{\delta_c}^{\delta_{max}}(P_e-P_m)\,d\delta\), after the fault is cleared.
  • Critical clearing angle: for a fault with \(P_e=0\) during the fault, setting \(A_1=A_2\) with \(\delta_{max}=\pi-\delta_0\) gives \(\cos\delta_{cr}=\dfrac{P_m}{P_{max}}(\pi-2\delta_0)-\cos\delta_0\).
  • Critical clearing time: the time taken to reach \(\delta_{cr}\). The fault must be cleared before this.
  • Use: circuit breakers are chosen to clear faults faster than the critical clearing time.

docs.title: Q7. Explain overcurrent, differential and distance protection. (5 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Overcurrent: the relay operates when the current exceeds a set value. It is simple and used on feeders, with time grading for coordination.
  • Differential: compares currents entering and leaving the protected zone. It operates when the difference exceeds a threshold, which means an internal fault.
  • Differential use: it is very selective and is used for transformers, generators and busbars.
  • Distance: measures the impedance \(V/I\) seen by the relay. A fault makes it fall below the set reach.
  • Distance use: the reach does not depend on source strength, so it is used on transmission lines, with zones 1, 2 and 3.

docs.title: Q8. Describe the types of circuit breakers and how the arc is extinguished. (5 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Function: a circuit breaker opens a circuit under fault and must interrupt the arc.
  • Arc extinction: the arc is extinguished at a current zero, by cooling it and raising the dielectric strength of the gap faster than the recovery voltage.
  • Air-blast: a high pressure air blast blows the arc away and cools it.
  • SF6: the gas has high dielectric strength and absorbs free electrons, so it is used for high voltages.
  • Vacuum: there is almost no medium to ionise, so the arc dies quickly. It is common at medium voltage.

docs.title: Q9. How are frequency and voltage controlled in a power system? (2 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Frequency: it follows the real power balance, so it is controlled by governors and automatic generation control.
  • Voltage: it follows reactive power, so it is controlled by capacitor banks, tap changing transformers, synchronous condensers and generator excitation.

docs.title: Q10. A load of 100 kW at 0.8 power factor lagging is to be improved to 0.95. Find the capacitor kVAR required. (5 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Formula: \(Q_c=P(\tan\phi_1-\tan\phi_2)\).
  • Initial angle: \(\cos\phi_1=0.8\), so \(\tan\phi_1=0.75\).
  • Final angle: \(\cos\phi_2=0.95\), so \(\tan\phi_2=0.329\).
  • Calculation: \(Q_c=100(0.75-0.329)\).
  • Answer: \(Q_c\approx42.1\) kVAR.

docs.title: Q11. What is the operator \(a\) and what are \(1+a+a^2\) and \(a^3\)? (2 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Definition: \(a=1\angle120^\circ=-0.5+j0.866\), and \(a^2=1\angle240^\circ\).
  • Properties: \(1+a+a^2=0\) and \(a^3=1\).

docs.title: Q12. Which fault is the most common and which is the most severe? (2 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Most common: the single line-to-ground fault, roughly 70 to 80 percent of faults.
  • Most severe: the symmetrical 3-phase fault, which usually gives the highest fault current, and it is used to size breakers.

docs.title: Q13. What is critical clearing time? (2 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Definition: the maximum time a fault can stay on the system before the generator loses synchronism.
  • Use: faults must be cleared faster than this for the system to remain stable.

docs.title: Q14. Why is the Y-bus matrix sparse? (2 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Reason: each bus is connected to only a few other buses, so most off-diagonal entries are zero.
  • Benefit: sparsity techniques save memory and time in load flow studies.

docs.title: Q15. What does a delta winding do to zero sequence currents? (2 marks · Module 1 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Trapping: zero sequence currents circulate inside a delta winding and cannot flow in the lines outside it.
  • Effect: the delta isolates the zero sequence network of the two sides of a transformer.

docs.title: Q16. Derive the output voltages of the buck, boost and buck-boost converters. (10 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Method: in steady state the average inductor voltage over one period is zero (volt-second balance).
  • Duty ratio: \(D=t_{on}/T\), where the switch is on for \(t_{on}\).
  • Buck, switch on: \(V_L=V_s-V_o\), for time \(DT\).
  • Buck, switch off: \(V_L=-V_o\), for time \((1-D)T\).
  • Buck result: balancing gives \(V_o=DV_s\), so it only steps down.
  • Boost, switch on: \(V_L=V_s\), for time \(DT\).
  • Boost, switch off: \(V_L=V_s-V_o\), for time \((1-D)T\).
  • Boost result: \(V_o=\dfrac{V_s}{1-D}\), so it only steps up.
  • Buck-boost: \(V_L=V_s\) when on and \(V_L=V_o\) when off, so \(V_o=-\dfrac{D}{1-D}V_s\).
  • Buck-boost result: the output is inverted and can be higher or lower than the input.

docs.title: Q17. A buck converter has \(V_s=24\) V, \(V_o=12\) V, \(L=100\ \mu\)H and \(f=50\) kHz. Find \(D\) and the inductor ripple current. (5 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Duty ratio: \(D=V_o/V_s=12/24=0.5\).
  • Ripple formula: \(\Delta I_L=\dfrac{(V_s-V_o)D}{fL}\).
  • Substitution: \(\Delta I_L=\dfrac{(24-12)\times0.5}{50\times10^3\times100\times10^{-6}}=\dfrac{6}{5}\).
  • Answer: the ripple current is \(1.2\) A peak to peak.
  • Boost check: a boost with \(V_s=12\) V and \(D=0.6\) gives \(V_o=12/0.4=30\) V.

docs.title: Q18. Derive the average output voltage of a single-phase fully controlled bridge rectifier with a highly inductive load. Find it for \(V_m=325\) V and \(\alpha=60^\circ\). (5 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Setup: each pair of thyristors conducts for 180° starting at the firing angle \(\alpha\).
  • Integration: \(V_{dc}=\dfrac1\pi\int_\alpha^{\pi+\alpha}V_m\sin\omega t\,d(\omega t)\).
  • Result: \(V_{dc}=\dfrac{2V_m}{\pi}\cos\alpha\).
  • Numerical: \(V_{dc}=\dfrac{2\times325}{\pi}\cos60^\circ=\dfrac{325}{\pi}\).
  • Answer: \(V_{dc}\approx103.4\) V. For \(\alpha>90^\circ\) the output is negative, so the converter works as an inverter.

docs.title: Q19. Find the average output of a three-phase uncontrolled bridge rectifier fed from a 415 V line-to-line supply. (5 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Formula: \(V_{dc}=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{\pi}V_{LL}\approx1.35\,V_{LL}\).
  • Source: it comes from averaging the highest line-to-line voltage over each 60° interval.
  • Substitution: \(V_{dc}=1.35\times415\).
  • Answer: \(V_{dc}\approx560\) V.
  • Controlled version: for a fully controlled bridge multiply by \(\cos\alpha\).

docs.title: Q20. Compare the thyristor, TRIAC, GTO, MOSFET and IGBT. (5 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Thyristor: latches on after a gate pulse and turns off only when the current falls to zero. It is used for high power.
  • TRIAC: a bidirectional thyristor used for AC control such as dimmers.
  • GTO: a thyristor that can also be turned off by a negative gate pulse, at high power.
  • MOSFET: voltage-controlled and very fast, used up to a few hundred volts and high frequencies.
  • IGBT: combines MOSFET gate drive with bipolar conduction, and is widely used for medium voltage and power in inverters.

docs.title: Q21. Explain the single-phase full-bridge inverter and sinusoidal PWM. (10 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Circuit: four switches in two legs, with an anti-parallel diode across each, supplied from a DC source \(V_{dc}\).
  • Square wave: switching diagonal pairs in turn gives an output of \(\pm V_{dc}\).
  • Square wave fundamental: its peak is \(\dfrac{4V_{dc}}{\pi}\), with large low-order harmonics.
  • Sinusoidal PWM: compare a sinusoidal reference with a high frequency triangular carrier to set the switching instants.
  • Rule: a switch is on when the reference is above the carrier, so the pulse widths vary sinusoidally.
  • Amplitude modulation index: \(m_a=\dfrac{V_{ref}}{V_{carrier}}\).
  • Linear range: for \(m_a\le1\) the fundamental output peak is \(m_aV_{dc}\).
  • Frequency modulation ratio: \(m_f=\dfrac{f_{carrier}}{f_{ref}}\).
  • Harmonics: they move to around multiples of the carrier frequency, so a small filter removes them.
  • Three-phase: use three references 120° apart with a common carrier, and the lines see balanced voltages.

docs.title: Q22. Define the power factor, distortion factor and THD of an AC to DC converter. (5 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Power factor: \(PF=\dfrac{P}{VI_{rms}}=DF\cdot\cos\phi_1\).
  • Distortion factor: \(DF=\dfrac{I_1}{I_{rms}}\), the ratio of the fundamental to the total rms current.
  • Displacement angle: \(\phi_1\) is the angle between the fundamental current and the voltage.
  • THD: \(THD=\dfrac{\sqrt{I_{rms}^2-I_1^2}}{I_1}\), and \(DF=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1+THD^2}}\).
  • Effect: line commutated converters draw non-sinusoidal current, so the power factor drops even if \(\cos\phi_1\) is 1.

docs.title: Q23. Differentiate latching current and holding current of a thyristor. (2 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Latching current: the minimum anode current needed to keep the thyristor on right after the gate pulse is removed.
  • Holding current: the minimum anode current below which an already conducting thyristor turns off. It is lower than the latching current.

docs.title: Q24. Which of the devices can be turned off by the gate? (2 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Gate turn-off devices: GTO, MOSFET and IGBT, plus the BJT.
  • Not gate-turn-off: a thyristor and a TRIAC turn off only when the current falls to zero.

docs.title: Q25. What is the purpose of a freewheeling diode? (2 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Path: it gives the inductive load current a path when the switch or rectifier output goes to zero.
  • Benefit: it prevents voltage spikes and improves the output waveform and power factor.

docs.title: Q26. What is the range of duty ratio of the boost converter and why must \(D<1\)? (2 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Range: \(0\le D<1\), and the gain is \(1/(1-D)\).
  • Limit: as \(D\to1\) the ideal gain goes to infinity, but real losses keep the practical limit at about \(D<0.8\).

docs.title: Q27. What is the difference between a line commutated converter and a self commutated converter? (2 marks · Module 2 · Mid Sem)
docs.text:
• Line commutated: the AC supply voltage turns the thyristors off, as in controlled rectifiers.
  • Self commutated: the devices turn off by their own gate control, as in IGBT inverters and choppers.
